plan: Social-science passage of about 600 words (CLD-P-ACT-R-000015) on the psychology of waiting; three hard items apply one paragraph's idea to another's example, with near-miss and counterintuitive distractors; the central felt-versus-actual contrast is the key of only one item.

passages.title: The Length of a Wait
passages.text:
Anyone who has waited in line knows that ten minutes can feel like five or like thirty. Operations researchers, who study how to make systems run efficiently, spent much of the twentieth century trying to shorten actual waits: adding servers, smoothing the flow of arrivals, predicting busy periods. Their work was valuable, but it rested on an assumption that turned out to be only half true: that what people mind about waiting is the time itself.

In the 1980s a business scholar named David Maister proposed that the experience of waiting depends at least as much on how a wait feels as on how long it lasts. Unoccupied time, he argued, feels longer than occupied time. Uncertain waits feel longer than waits of known length, and unexplained waits feel longer than explained ones. People waiting alone notice the time more than people waiting in groups, and a wait that seems unfair, with someone who arrived later being served first, feels longer than an equal wait that seems fair.

Some of the most cited applications of these ideas cost almost nothing. When passengers at one airport complained about long waits for their luggage, the airport moved arriving flights to gates farther from the baggage claim. Passengers now spent most of the interval walking instead of standing, and complaints dropped, although the total time from plane to bag stayed about the same. Mirrors in elevator lobbies, which give waiting people something to look at, are often explained in the same way.

Not everyone is comfortable with this approach. Critics point out that a company can use the psychology of waiting to avoid fixing the underlying problem: a theme park that entertains people in a ninety-minute line has made the wait more bearable without making it any shorter. In their view, distraction manages customers' perceptions instead of respecting their time.

Defenders reply that the two goals are not in competition. Shortening a wait often requires expensive changes, such as hiring staff or building new facilities, that take years to complete; making a wait feel shorter can be done tomorrow. A hospital that posts estimated waiting times in its emergency room, they note, has not reduced those times, but it has removed one of the main sources of distress for patients who must wait regardless.

Perhaps the most intriguing finding is how little the clock seems to matter in memory. Studies of people leaving lines suggest that their satisfaction depends heavily on how the wait ended and on whether it moved steadily, rather than on its total length. A line that advances a little at a time can be remembered more kindly than a shorter one that stalls and then lurches forward. If waiting is partly a story we tell ourselves afterward, then the people who design lines are, in a sense, also its authors.

candidates.stem: The author most likely calls the operations researchers' assumption "only half true" (paragraph 1) because:

choices.A: operations researchers seldom managed to make the waits they studied any shorter.
choices.B: people care more about the fairness of a wait than about any other feature of it.
choices.C: the length of a wait matters, but so do features such as uncertainty and fairness.
choices.D: most people greatly overestimate how long they have actually spent waiting.

candidates.evidence: depends at least as much on how a wait feels as on how long it lasts
candidates.explanation: "Half true" means time matters but is not all that matters. Paragraph 2 supplies the other half: how a wait feels, shaped by uncertainty, fairness, company and occupation.

A.rationale: The author calls their work "valuable"; the problem was the assumption, not failure.

B.rationale: Fairness is one of several features listed; nothing ranks it above the rest.

D.rationale: The passage never says people misjudge the length of their waits.

hints: What does paragraph 2 add to the idea that people mind the time itself?
candidates.remember: "Half true": find what the passage keeps and what it adds.

author_checklist.hardness: Requires reading "half true" as "true but incomplete" and supplying the missing half from the next paragraph; B overstates one feature.

candidates.subskill: Applying one group's view to an example
candidates.stem: The critics described in paragraph 4 would most likely regard the airport's change described in paragraph 3 as:

choices.A: a way of improving how the wait felt without dealing with how long it actually took.
choices.B: an unfair practice, because it made passengers' total waiting time noticeably longer.
choices.C: a good example of a company that chose to respect its customers' time.
choices.D: an irrelevant case, because passengers who are walking are not really waiting.

candidates.evidence: distraction manages customers' perceptions instead of respecting their time
candidates.explanation: The critics object to making a wait more bearable without shortening it, which is exactly what the airport did: the time stayed the same while complaints dropped.

B.rationale: The total time from plane to bag "stayed about the same."

C.rationale: The critics argue that such changes manage perceptions instead of respecting time.

D.rationale: The critics' objection concerns perceptions versus actual time, not whether walking counts as waiting.

hints: What did the airport change, and what stayed the same?
What do the critics object to?

strategy.explanation: Apply paragraph 4's view to paragraph 3's example.

candidates.remember: Applying a viewpoint: match the example to the group's stated objection.

author_checklist.hardness: Requires applying the critics' general objection to an example from another paragraph; C reverses their view.

candidates.subskill: Connecting an example to an earlier idea
candidates.stem: Posting estimated waiting times in an emergency room (paragraph 5) most directly addresses which feature of waiting described in paragraph 2?

choices.A: Waiting alone rather than with other people
choices.B: Not knowing how long the wait will last
choices.C: Seeing someone who arrived later served first
choices.D: Having nothing to occupy one's attention

candidates.evidence: Uncertain waits feel longer than waits of known length
candidates.explanation: An estimated waiting time turns an uncertain wait into one of roughly known length, the feature Maister says makes waits feel shorter.

A.rationale: Posting times does not change whether patients wait alone.

C.rationale: Posted times do not address the order of service.

D.rationale: Posted times give information, not something to do.

hints: What do patients learn from a posted time?

strategy.explanation: Match the example to one feature in paragraph 2.

candidates.remember: Link examples back to the specific principle they illustrate.

candidates.stem: Based on paragraph 6, which of the following lines would most likely be remembered more favorably?

choices.A: A 15-minute line that does not move for 10 minutes and then empties quickly
choices.B: A 12-minute line that moves steadily at first and then stops for the last 8 minutes
choices.C: A 25-minute line that alternates between long stops and sudden bursts of movement
choices.D: A 20-minute line that advances a few steps every minute until the end

candidates.evidence: A line that advances a little at a time can be remembered more kindly than a shorter one
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 6 says steady movement and a good ending matter more than total length. The 20-minute steady line beats shorter lines that stall.

A.rationale: This line stalls and then lurches forward, the pattern remembered less kindly.

B.rationale: Satisfaction depends heavily on how the wait ended; this one ends with a stall.

C.rationale: This line neither moves steadily nor ends well.

hints: According to paragraph 6, what matters more than total length?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate lines that stall or end badly.

candidates.remember: Apply the passage's criteria, even when they defy intuition.

author_checklist.hardness: The counterintuitive answer is not the shortest line; three distractors are shorter or longer but stall or end badly.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 6, the word "lurches" most nearly means:
candidates.explanation: After stalling, the line moves forward in a sudden, uneven jerk: it "lurches."

A.rationale: The line has already stalled; "lurches forward" describes what happens next.

B.rationale: This familiar sense of "lurch" does not describe a line moving forward.

D.rationale: Steady movement is contrasted with stalling and lurching.

hints: What does the line do just before it lurches?
candidates.remember: Use the contrast in the sentence to fix a word's meaning.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the author's attitude toward Maister's ideas about waiting?

choices.A: The author treats them as insightful and influential while acknowledging a debate about how they are used.
choices.B: The author doubts them and suggests that only the actual length of a wait matters to people.
choices.C: The author argues that they make it unnecessary for any business to shorten its customers' waits.
choices.D: The author reports them without expressing any view about their importance or their usefulness.

candidates.explanation: The author builds on Maister's ideas, gives examples of their influence, presents both sides of the debate over their use and calls one finding "most intriguing."

B.rationale: The author calls the time-only assumption "only half true."

C.rationale: The author presents both critics and defenders and does not claim shortening is unnecessary.

D.rationale: Phrases such as "most intriguing finding" show the author's interest and engagement.

hints: Does the author ever reject Maister's ideas?
Where does the author show a personal reaction?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate attitudes contradicted by the author's word choices.

candidates.remember: Attitude: look for evaluative words, not just topics.

candidates.stem: In the final sentence, the author's claim that the people who design lines are "also its authors" most nearly means that they:

choices.A: write the rules that customers must follow while they are waiting in line.
choices.B: shape the experience people later recall, not just the time people spend.
choices.C: ask customers to write about their experiences after leaving a line.
choices.D: alone decide how long every wait will last for each customer in line.

candidates.evidence: If waiting is partly a story we tell ourselves afterward
candidates.explanation: If a wait is remembered as a story, then those who control how it moves and ends help write that story.

A.rationale: "Authors" is figurative; the passage is not about written rules.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests designers collect written accounts.

D.rationale: The sentence concerns the remembered story of a wait, not control over its length.

hints: What does the "if" clause say waiting partly is?
candidates.remember: Figurative claims: follow the metaphor set up just before them.

candidates.stem: According to paragraph 2, Maister argued that a wait feels longer when:

choices.A: a person who arrived later is served before others.
choices.B: a person waits in a large group of friends.
choices.C: a person is told exactly how long the wait will be.
choices.D: a person has something to occupy the time.

candidates.evidence: someone who arrived later being served first
candidates.explanation: Maister says an unfair wait, such as someone later being served first, feels longer.

B.rationale: Maister says waiting alone, not in a group, feels longer.

C.rationale: Waits of known length feel shorter, not longer.

hints: Which choice describes an unfair wait?
candidates.remember: Detail questions: the answer is stated in the passage.
